page_title: Writing summaries is more important than reading more books — Andreas Fragner

sources.entry: Writing summaries is more important than reading more books

summary.title: Writing summaries is more important than reading more books
summary.one_liner: Read fewer books, but write a short question-based synopsis of the good ones, and use topical and inspectional reading to choose which books are worth your time.
keywords: how to remember what you read
adler and van doren how to read a book
takeaways: Spend time writing a synopsis of good books; the return on that time is higher than reading another book.
Optimize reading for comprehension rather than page count or speed.
Ask questions while reading, then write a synopsis: book overview, 3-4 central questions with answers, and personal takeaways.
Use topical reading to pick 4-5 topics per quarter, then inspectional reading (preface, table of contents, chapter summaries) to cut the list to about 2 books per topic.
Explaining a book's ideas to someone else is an alternative way to engage with it; speed reading is largely a trade-off against comprehension, per the author.
summary.summary: The author argues that reading fewer books and writing synopses for the good ones yields more than reading volume. He recommends a four-part synopsis template built around questions the book answers. He describes two selection techniques: topical reading to gather works on chosen topics each quarter, and inspectional reading (skimming the blurb, preface, table of contents and chapter summaries, roughly an hour) to narrow each list to about two books. He also notes that speed reading involves a hard trade-off against comprehension, and cites Adler and Van Doren's How to Read a Book.
